metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate difficulty: teenager (18F) with initially normal MRI, referred as first-episode psychosis. Key moderate challenge is that MRI is near-normal (subtle), EEG shows only generalised slowing without diagnostic features, and CSF changes are mild. Antibody confirmation required. Ovarian teratoma found on ultrasound.

patient.presenting_complaint: Four-week history of behavioural change, paranoia, and sleep disturbance followed by a witnessed seizure
patient.hpi: An 18-year-old A-level student was brought to the emergency department by her parents following a generalised tonic-clonic seizure at home. Her parents had been concerned for approximately four weeks during which she had progressively withdrawn from her schoolwork and social activities. Her mother reported that she had become increasingly fearful, frequently stating that someone was watching her through the windows, and had refused to sleep in her own room. She had begun to hallucinate auditory stimuli — hearing voices commenting on her actions — which she disclosed tearfully to her mother approximately two weeks prior to admission. In the two weeks before presentation, she had not attended school, rarely left her bedroom, and was sleeping for only two to three hours per night. Two A-level teachers and her school counsellor had noted the dramatic change from her previously high-achieving, sociable character. A&E had been attended once ten days prior where a junior doctor had assessed her, attributed the presentation to adolescent psychosis versus drug misuse, and arranged emergency CAMHS follow-up (not yet seen). Her parents vehemently denied any substance misuse and noted that prior to this illness she had been a high-performing student with no personal or family history of mental health problems. On the morning of admission she had an approximately two-minute convulsive episode during which she was unresponsive and bit her tongue. There was urinary incontinence during the seizure. She denied any illicit drug use. She has no significant past medical history. Family history is unremarkable.
pmh: Mild upper respiratory tract infection 5 weeks prior to onset — resolved without treatment

family_history: No family history of psychiatric, neurological, or autoimmune disease.

social_history.note: A-level student (biology, chemistry, maths). High academic achiever prior to illness. Lives with parents and two younger siblings. Non-smoker, no alcohol, no illicit drugs confirmed by urine screen. Not sexually active per parental report.

past_medical_history: Mild upper respiratory tract infection 5 weeks prior to onset — resolved without treatment

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert but agitated and intermittently uncooperative. Disoriented to time. Expresses paranoid ideation that hospital staff are going to 'experiment' on her. Auditory hallucinations ongoing. Intermittent mutism. No formal cognitive assessment possible.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 5mm, equal, and reactive. Orofacial dyskinesias noted — episodic tongue protrusion and chewing movements not corresponding to voluntary activity. Fundoscopy deferred (uncooperative).
neurological_exam.motor: Power 5/5 all limbs. No focal weakness. Tone normal.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Brisk throughout. Bilateral plantar flexor responses.
neurological_exam.coordination: Unable to cooperate with cerebellar testing.

red_herrings.intended_effect: MRI negative excludes encephalitis — diagnosis is primary psychiatric disorder
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: MRI is normal in up to 50% of anti-NMDAR encephalitis cases. Normal MRI does NOT exclude the diagnosis. CSF changes and antibody positivity are the key diagnostic tests.

red_herrings.data_point: Adolescent presenting with auditory hallucinations and paranoia
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: New-onset seizure in a psychiatric presentation should always prompt encephalitis workup. Orofacial dyskinesias (tongue protrusion, lip smacking) are not features of primary psychosis. CSF pleocytosis and antibodies confirm autoimmune aetiology.

red_herrings.data_point: Normal drug screen and no substance use
red_herrings.intended_effect: Substance misuse excluded — diagnosis defaults to psychiatric
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Negative drug screen is expected; it excludes one differential but does not provide a positive diagnosis. The pattern of progressive encephalopathy over 4 weeks requires a mechanistic explanation — autoimmune encephalitis is that explanation.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis with left ovarian mature teratoma, adolescent female

differential.key_features: CSF pleocytosis, oligoclonal bands, orofacial dyskinesias, seizures, and hyponatraemia are not features of primary psychosis. Anti-NMDAR antibodies confirmed.
Urine drug screen negative. Parents and school confirm no substance use history.
HSV PCR negative. Near-normal MRI (no haemorrhagic temporal changes). 4-week subacute course inconsistent with HSV.
Normal TSH, normal anti-TPO antibodies. Anti-NMDAR antibodies confirmed.

optimal_actions.action: MRI brain — evaluate for encephalitis, exclude structural lesion
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Near-normal MRI — subtle right amygdalar change. Normal MRI does not exclude anti-NMDAR encephalitis.

optimal_actions.action: EEG — assess for encephalopathic pattern or subclinical seizures
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Diffuse encephalopathic slowing inappropriate for age — supports organic rather than psychiatric diagnosis

optimal_actions.action: Lumbar puncture — CSF analysis, viral PCR, autoimmune encephalitis antibodies
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Mild lymphocytic pleocytosis, borderline protein, oligoclonal bands, anti-NMDAR antibodies pending

optimal_actions.action: Send anti-NMDAR antibodies serum and CSF; full autoimmune encephalitis panel
Pelvic ultrasound for ovarian teratoma screening
Initiate first-line immunotherapy — IVMP 1g/day × 5 days and IVIG 2 g/kg over 5 days
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Standard first-line immunotherapy for anti-NMDAR encephalitis

optimal_actions.action: Refer to paediatric gynaecology for laparoscopic oophorectomy
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Tumour removal improves neurological outcomes — mandatory in teratoma-positive cases

critical_actions: Normal MRI does NOT exclude anti-NMDAR encephalitis — up to 50% of cases have normal MRI
Abnormal EEG in an adolescent presenting with psychiatric symptoms is an organic red flag
Anti-NMDAR antibodies must be sent in both CSF and serum — CSF is more sensitive
Pelvic ultrasound mandatory in all females with anti-NMDAR encephalitis (regardless of age)
Left ovarian teratoma must be removed — laparoscopic oophorectomy improves long-term neurological outcomes
contraindicated_actions: Discharge to CAMHS as first-episode psychosis without CSF and MRI workup when seizures have occurred
Use antipsychotics as primary treatment without addressing autoimmune cause
Delay immunotherapy awaiting antibody confirmation in clinically convincing presentation with seizures
key_reasoning_points: The combination of psychiatric prodrome + seizures + orofacial dyskinesias in a young female should always trigger encephalitis workup — this clinical triad is the hallmark of anti-NMDAR encephalitis.
Normal MRI is present in 50% of anti-NMDAR encephalitis. The diagnosis is fundamentally serological, not radiological.
Encephalopathic EEG (diffuse slowing) in an otherwise healthy 18-year-old is a strong red flag for organic brain disease — primary psychiatric disorders produce normal EEGs.
Hyponatraemia in the context of encephalitis with psychiatric features suggests hypothalamic involvement (SIADH) — this supports rather than detracts from the anti-NMDAR diagnosis.
Ovarian teratoma detection and removal is the single most important prognostic intervention — all young females with anti-NMDAR encephalitis require pelvic imaging regardless of MRI findings.

findings.location: Medial temporal lobe (left hippocampus and amygdala)

mri.impression: Essentially normal MRI. Possible extremely subtle right amygdalar asymmetry — not diagnostic; may represent a normal variant. No mass, hemorrhage, restricted diffusion, or pathological enhancement. Clinical correlation recommended.

background.posterior_dominant_rhythm: Poorly organized theta activity, 6-7 Hz, replacing expected alpha rhythm

findings.morphology: Generalised theta slowing (6-7 Hz). No posterior dominant rhythm. Diffusely disorganised for age (expected alpha dominant 9-10 Hz in an 18-year-old).
No focal temporal epileptiform discharges. No rhythmic delta activity.
No extreme delta brush. No ictal activity captured. Diffuse encephalopathy pattern — non-specific but inappropriate for a healthy adolescent.

eeg.impression: Abnormal EEG for age — diffuse encephalopathic slowing without localising features. Clinical correlation recommended.

labs.interpretation: Abnormal values: Sodium 129 mEq/L (L), Chloride 97 mEq/L (L), CRP 0.8 mg/dL (H), ESR 22 mm/hr (H), CK 148 U/L (H).

csf.interpretation: Opening pressure: 17 cmH2O. Protein: 0.48 g/L. Glucose: 3.2 mmol/L.

output.interpretation: Abnormal values: Serum anti-NMDA receptor IgG Weakly positive (titer 1:20) (H), CSF anti-NMDA receptor IgG Positive (titer 1:40) (H). Anti-NMDA receptor IgG antibody is found in a subset of patients with autoimmune encephalitis; a positive result should be interpreted in the clinical context. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.query: Anti-NMDAR encephalitis paediatric adolescent management guidelines

results.title: Anti-NMDAR encephalitis in children and adolescents
results.summary: Presentation in children/adolescents may differ from adults: more common movement disorders (choreiform movements), more prominent behavioural features, seizures more prominent than autonomic instability. Teratoma association lower in prepubertal girls but rises with age. Immunotherapy protocol similar to adults: IVMP + IVIG first-line. Long-term neurodevelopmental follow-up essential — cognitive and psychiatric sequelae common. School re-integration planning required.

output.mechanism: Antipsychotics are frequently prescribed for the psychiatric phase of anti-NMDAR encephalitis, mistaking it for first-episode psychosis. Risk: NMS-like reactions; also masks progression of encephalitis. If required for behavioural safety, use lowest effective dose with ECG monitoring (QTc). Benzodiazepines preferred for acute agitation.
output.recommendation: Avoid antipsychotics if anti-NMDAR encephalitis suspected. Use lorazepam for acute agitation. Discuss with paediatric neurology.
